intro: Hokuto's hero tree is Jindai-zakura, the oldest of Japan's Three Great Cherry Trees and, by tradition, the oldest cherry in the country: somewhere between 1,800 and 2,000 years old, named a National Natural Monument in 1922. A second cherry, Shinden no Oitozakura, stands alone in a rice paddy 7.5km away and once told farmers when to plant. A third tree, a designated wild azalea near the summit of Mt Utsukushimori, hides among a much larger, undesignated blaze of colour that draws most of the crowd past it.
meta_description: Hokuto's three mapped trees: Jindai-zakura, by tradition Japan's oldest cherry, a paddy-field cherry, and a National Monument azalea on Mt Utsukushimori.
question_answer: Hokuto's oldest mapped tree is Jindai-zakura, an Edo-higan cherry at Jisso-ji Temple traditionally estimated at 1,800 to 2,000 years old, which would make it the oldest cherry tree in Japan. The figure rests on a legend that the warrior prince Yamato Takeru planted it, repeated by tourism boards and government publications but backed by no dating method, so read it as tradition rather than measurement.
question_meta: Jindai-zakura in Hokuto is traditionally called Japan's oldest cherry tree, at up to 2,000 years. One of the Three Great Cherry Trees.
question_context: Jindai-zakura grows on the grounds of Jisso-ji Temple in Yamataka, a hamlet in the city of Hokuto at the foot of the Southern Japan Alps. In October 1922 the Japanese government named its first National Natural Monuments, and this cherry was one of only five individual trees on that inaugural list, alongside Miharu Takizakura and Usuzumi-zakura, the two trees it is now always grouped with as the Three Great Cherry Trees of Japan. The traditional age, 1,800 to 2,000 years, comes from a legend that the warrior prince Yamato Takeru planted it on his way through the region; no dating method backs the figure, and the trunk is too hollow and knotted to read reliably. What can be measured is the base, a root flare given as 11.8 to 13.5 metres round beneath a tree only about 10 metres tall, spreading outward rather than climbing. Bloom forecasters track it individually every spring, and seeds from it have reportedly been flown into space and grown on in gardens abroad.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Hokuto?
faq.a: Jindai-zakura, at Jisso-ji Temple. By tradition it is 1,800 to 2,000 years old, and Japanese sources often call it the oldest cherry tree in the country, though the figure rests on legend rather than a dating method.

Jindai means the age of the gods. Local legend credits the warrior prince Yamato Takeru with planting it on his way through the region, which is also where the traditional age comes from, a legend rather than a measurement.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: Early April, when the pale, drooping blossom typical of Edo-higan cherries opens. Bloom forecasters track the tree individually each spring.
Jisso-ji Temple charges a small entry fee, around 500 yen, during blossom season; some listings describe it as free the rest of the year, so check locally. The grounds are open to the public.

faq.q: What is the second tree Hokuto maps?
faq.a: Shinden no Oitozakura, a weeping Higan cherry standing alone at the edge of a rice paddy in Kobuchisawa, about 7.5km from Jindai-zakura. A Yamanashi Prefecture Natural Monument since 1959.

faq.q: What is the third tree Hokuto maps?
faq.a: Utsukushimori no Oyamatsutsuji, a single National Natural Monument azalea near the summit of Mt Utsukushimori, distinct from the much larger undesignated blaze of wild azaleas covering the same hillside.

trees.name: Jindai-zakura (Yamataka Jindai Zakura)

location.address: Jisso-ji Temple, 2763 Yamataka, Takegawa-cho, Hokuto-shi, Yamanashi 408-0306, Japan

trees.story:
In October 1922 Japan named its first National Natural Monuments. Five single trees were on that list, and this cherry was one of them. It is also counted among the Three Great Cherry Trees of Japan, with Miharu Takizakura in Fukushima and Usuzumi-zakura in Gifu, both designated on the very same day.

The age usually given is 1,800 to 2,000 years, tied to a legend that the warrior prince Yamato Takeru planted it. Treat that as a tradition rather than a finding. The prefecture's tourism board, the city of Hokuto and a government cultural publication all repeat the figure and none cites a dating method, and the trunk is too hollow and knotted to read reliably. What can be measured is the base: a root flare given as 11.8 metres round by the prefecture and 13.5 by other listings, under a tree only about 10 metres tall. It grows outward rather than up.

It is an Edo-higan, the long-lived species behind many of Japan's oldest cherries, and the blossom is pale and drooping in early April. Bloom forecasters still track this individual tree season by season, which is how we know it is alive and watched. Seeds from it have reportedly been flown into space and grown on around the world.

Jisso-ji charges around 500 yen during blossom season. Without a car it is a taxi from Hinoharu or Kobuchizawa.

best_time.label: early April, when the pale drooping blossom opens

trees.access: Paid entry to Jisso-ji Temple grounds during blossom season (approx 500 yen adult, per Japanese-language tourism sources); free rest of year per some listings, so check locally. Grounds are open to the public.
trees.transport: Nearest station is JR Chuo Main Line's Hinoharu, then taxi or the Hokuto municipal bus (Mukawa loop line) to the Jindai Koen stop; from Kobuchizawa station it is roughly a 30-minute taxi ride.

trees.name: Shinden no Oitozakura
trees.species: Weeping Higan Cherry (Prunus subhirtella var. pendula)

location.address: Matsumuki, Kobuchisawa-cho, Hokuto City, Yamanashi Prefecture 408-0042, Japan

trees.story:
Before calendars told Kobuchisawa's farmers when to plant rice, this cherry did. Tradition holds it was planted as a goshinboku, a sacred tree, on the paddy-field ridge that once grew rice offered to a shrine, and its bloom timing served as the signal to begin planting season.

It stands alone at the edge of a working rice paddy at about 820 metres elevation, the kind of solitary specimen that gets used for film and tourism location scouting rather than crowded up by other trees. A weeping form of the Edo Higan cherry, it is thought to have taken root around the shift from the Sengoku era to the Edo period, putting it at roughly 400 years old, a figure that lines up with what a tree this size should be.

Sources differ slightly on the trunk: the city gives 8 metres round, the tourism board a more precise 7.5. The smaller figure is used here.

It was designated a Yamanashi Prefecture Natural Monument in 1959, prefectural rather than national. Free parking for about 30 cars and 5 buses sits nearby. Close approach has been temporarily restricted in places while the soil and roots recover from foot traffic, though the tree stays visible from the paddy edge and the parking area throughout.

best_time.label: April, when it blooms and once signalled the start of rice planting

trees.access: Free. Stands alone at the edge of a working rice paddy at about 820m elevation; dedicated free parking (about 30 cars, 5 buses) is provided nearby. Close approach may be temporarily restricted in places while soil and root recovery work continues, though the tree remains visible from the paddy edge and parking area.
trees.transport: 10 minutes by taxi from JR Kobuchisawa Station, or 12 minutes from JR Nagasaka Station; also reachable by municipal bus line 1 (about 10 min) plus a 10-minute walk from the 'Hara Village' stop.

trees.name: Utsukushimori no Oyamatsutsuji

location.address: 8240-1 Nishi-ide, Oizumi-cho, Hokuto City, Yamanashi Prefecture, on Mt Utsukushimori (Utsukushi-mori, 1,542m) on the southern foot of Mt Yatsugatake, near the hill's summit

trees.access: Free. Free parking at the base (about 50 cars, 4 buses) with a visitor centre, then roughly a 15-minute walk on a hiking trail up to the summit area of Mt Utsukushimori.
trees.transport: 5-minute drive from JR Koumi Line's Kiyosato Station, or 15 minutes from the Chuo Expressway's Nagasaka IC, then a ~15-minute walk from the base car park to the summit area.
trees.story:
The famous thing on this hill is not the protected thing. Mt Utsukushimori, 1,542 metres on the southern foot of Yatsugatake, carries something like a thousand rengetsutsuji that colour the whole slope in June and fill everyone's photographs. Those are a different species and none of them is designated. The National Natural Monument here is one azalea, listed on 7 June 1935, and most people walk straight past it.

The 1935 text tells you what to look for: a plant that divides at ground level into more than a dozen stems off a single root crown, those stems measuring about 2.7 metres round taken together, throwing a crown roughly six metres east to west and five and a half north to south. The 2.7 is a sum, not a trunk, which is worth knowing before you go up expecting something thick.

Nobody recorded an age in 1935 and nobody has since, so there is no age to give. Its current vigour is a fair question too: one unverified summary says the plant has been in decline, and no source we could check repeats it. Yamanashi Prefecture still listed it as a standing monument in April 2025.

It is a fifteen-minute walk up from the car park at the base, where there is a visitor centre and room for fifty cars. If you get up there and photograph the designated one rather than the hillside, send it to us.
